questions.prompt: Where does the JDBC driver jar (e.g. the PostgreSQL driver) go?
options: lib/ext only for plugins, never lib
questions.explanation: JDBC drivers go in lib (or are added via the Test Plan classpath). lib/ext is for JMeter plugins/components.

questions.prompt: Which Query Type should you use for a SELECT with ? placeholders?
questions.explanation: Prepared Select with parameter values and types runs parameterised reads. Update is for writes, Callable for stored procedures.

questions.prompt: The JDBC Request's 'Variable Name of Pool' must match the Variable Name in the JDBC Connection Configuration.
questions.explanation: That name links the sampler to its connection pool.

questions.prompt: Which built-in samplers exist for non-HTTP protocols? Pick the one that is NOT built in.
questions.explanation: JMS, TCP and LDAP samplers ship with JMeter. gRPC needs a plugin.

questions.prompt: Why are prepared statements preferred in JDBC load tests?
options: The database can reuse the plan, which matches how applications query, and parameters avoid SQL injection and string-building errors
They make the DB return cached rows only
questions.explanation: Applications normally use prepared statements; testing the same pattern gives realistic plan caching. JMeter also supports plain statements.

questions.prompt: When does testing the database directly with JDBC make sense? Select all that apply.
options: Isolating whether slow queries or the app layer cause latency
Validating a new index under concurrent load
questions.explanation: Direct DB tests isolate the database. They complement but do not replace end-to-end tests through the application.

questions.prompt: A JDBC test with 100 threads and pool Max Number of Connections 10 shows response times rising steeply while DB CPU is 20%. What is happening?
options: Threads wait for one of 10 pooled connections; the pool, not the database, limits throughput. Size the pool to match the app's real pool
questions.explanation: Low DB CPU with high waiting time indicates client-side pool contention. Missing drivers fail outright.

questions.prompt: A JDBC Update test inserts 1 million rows during the run. What should the plan include?
options: Test data cleanup (tearDown Thread Group or a script) and a note on how data growth affects later runs
Run it on production for realism
questions.explanation: Leftover data skews later tests and fills disks. Production testing of writes is unsafe, and updates are allowed.

coding.title: Find slow queries
coding.prompt: A table `query_log(query_name TEXT, elapsed_ms INTEGER, success INTEGER)` holds JDBC samples. Write a query returning `query_name`, `samples`, `avg_ms` (average rounded to the nearest integer with `ROUND(AVG(...))` cast to INTEGER) and `failures` for queries whose average is over 200 ms, **ordered by `avg_ms` descending**.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT * FROM query_log;
coding.solution:
SELECT query_name,
       COUNT(*) AS samples,
       CAST(ROUND(AVG(elapsed_ms)) AS INTEGER) AS avg_ms,
       SUM(CASE WHEN success = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS failures
FROM query_log
GROUP BY query_name
HAVING AVG(elapsed_ms) > 200
ORDER BY avg_ms DESC;
coding.explanation: GROUP BY gives one row per query, HAVING filters on the aggregate (WHERE cannot), and a CASE inside SUM counts failures. This is the kind of query you run on JDBC or APM data to rank bottlenecks.
hints: Count failures with `SUM(CASE WHEN success = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

coding.title: Validate test data integrity
coding.prompt: After a JDBC load test that created orders, check integrity. Tables: `orders(id INTEGER, customer_id INTEGER, total REAL)` and `customers(id INTEGER, name TEXT)`. Write a query returning the `id` of every order whose `customer_id` has no matching customer **or** whose `total` is negative or NULL. Return one column `id`, any order.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT name FROM customers;
coding.solution:
SELECT o.id
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.id IS NULL OR o.total IS NULL OR o.total < 0;
coding.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every order and leaves customer columns NULL when there is no match, so `c.id IS NULL` finds orphans. Checking NULL explicitly matters because `NULL < 0` is not true.
hints: Use a LEFT JOIN from orders to customers.
Orphans have `c.id IS NULL` after the join.
Add `OR o.total IS NULL OR o.total < 0`.
